opus-5.5.text:
I think the core question is: when would "it works on the cases we checked" fail to tell you what you actually care about? For a lot of behaviors, testing is basically fine. If a model translates French well on a big, representative sample, and the deployment distribution looks like that sample, I'm not that worried about why it works.

The behaviors where I want an explanation are the ones where the reason matters for whether it keeps working. The clearest case is when you can't check the thing directly. Take "the model tells me the truth" or "the model isn't tampering with the sensors that measure whether it did a good job." On the training distribution, two very different mechanisms produce the same observed behavior. One is "the model is actually trying to be honest." The other is "the model is saying whatever the overseer will rate highly, which happens to be the truth on cases where the overseer can tell." Those look identical until you hit a case where they come apart. And the cases where they come apart are exactly the high-stakes ones, where the model is smarter than you or there's an opportunity to do something bad without getting caught.

So my rough heuristic is: you need an explanation when there's a plausible alternative mechanism that would produce the same behavior on everything you can test but would diverge somewhere that matters. If you can't rule out that alternative by checking outcomes, you need to rule it out by understanding why the behavior happens.

That's a lot of the motivation for the work on things like mechanistic anomaly detection. You don't necessarily need a full human-legible story of the whole network. You want something like: here's the explanation for why the model behaved well on the training set. On a new input, is the model still behaving well for that same reason, or is something different going on? If the usual explanation stops applying, that's a flag, even if the output looks fine. The output looking fine is exactly what you'd expect in the scary case.

The other place I want explanations is rare events. If something catastrophic happens one in a million times, you won't see it in testing. To get any confidence, you need a reason to believe the bad behavior can't happen, or is very unlikely, rather than an empirical observation that it didn't happen in the samples you drew.

So it's not that every successful behavior needs an explanation. It's that alignment is disproportionately concerned with the behaviors where checking is unreliable: either you can't evaluate the outcome, or the failure is too rare to sample, or the system might be adversarially optimizing against your checks. Those are precisely the cases where "it works" isn't evidence of very much on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says testing is basically fine for many behaviors and that not every successful behavior needs an explanation, as long as outcomes can be checked reliably.

r002.rationale: It selects behaviors for explanation based on unreliable checking, plausible alternative mechanisms, and rare failures—not on how surprising the behavior is.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention GPT-4, its parameter count, or correct answers arising by coincidence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that for most of the behaviors you care about, you don't need an explanation. If my code sorts a list and I've tested it on a thousand inputs, I don't need a proof. The question is really about where testing fails, and testing fails in a pretty specific set of places.

The first is when the situations you care about aren't the ones you can test. You can check that a model behaves well when you're watching, but the thing you actually care about is what it does when you're not, or when it's in a position where its interests and yours have come apart. If a system is smart enough to tell those cases apart, then the test is measuring the wrong thing, and no amount of passing it should reassure you. That's the case where I think you genuinely need to understand why the behavior is happening and not just that it's happening.

The second is when the failure is rare but catastrophic. If something goes wrong one time in a million and the cost of that one time is enormous, you're never going to see it in your evaluation, and so you have to reason about it rather than observe it.

And the third, which I think people underrate, is when there are multiple mechanisms that would produce the same successful behavior but generalize very differently. A model that does what you want because it has internalized something like your goals and a model that does what you want because it has learned that this is what gets rewarded look identical on the training distribution. They look identical on most of the test distribution. They come apart exactly in the places you can't check. So when there's a plausible alternative story that fits all the evidence and leads somewhere bad, that's when "it works" stops being enough.

So my rough heuristic is: ask whether there's a cheap, bad explanation for the success that you can't rule out empirically. If there isn't, go ahead and just check that it works. If there is, you need to do the harder thing, which is actually understand what's producing the behavior. And a lot of my worry about the current trajectory is that the second category is where the most important behaviors sit, and it's also where our tools are weakest.

r001.rationale: The response says that for most behaviors, an explanation is unnecessary if direct testing shows they work.

r002.rationale: It selects behaviors for explanation based on limits of testing, catastrophic rare failures, or plausible harmful mechanisms—not on how surprising the behavior is.

r003.rationale: It does not mention GPT-4, its parameter count, or correct answers occurring by coincidence.

astra-6.text:
I think the main question is whether the behavior could change in a way that matters when you move to a setting where you can’t check it. If I can reliably check whether the system did what I wanted, then I don’t necessarily need a deeper explanation. I can just check.

But suppose I train a model to write code, and on all the examples I look at, the code has no security vulnerabilities. There are different explanations for that. Maybe the model is trying to write secure code. Maybe it’s producing code that passes the particular checks I use. Those explanations agree on the cases I’ve tested, but they can disagree on more complicated cases where my checks are inadequate.

So I don’t think you need to explain every successful behavior. You need enough evidence to distinguish between explanations that have different implications for what you’re going to do next. And the more you’re relying on the system in situations where you can’t evaluate its work, the more important that distinction becomes.

r001.rationale: It says that when a behavior can be reliably checked, a deeper explanation may not be needed; direct checking can be enough.

r002.rationale: It selects behaviors for explanation based on whether they may matter in settings where they cannot be checked, not on how surprising they are.

r003.rationale: It does not mention GPT-4, its parameter count, or correct answers occurring by coincidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you want to infer from the success. If you just want to know whether the system works in the particular conditions you tested, then checking that it works can be enough. But usually we want to make some further inference, like that it will continue to work in a new situation, or when it has more opportunities to do something bad. Then you need some account of why the behavior you observed is evidence for that claim.

For example, suppose a model tells you the truth in all the cases where you can check its answers. One explanation is that it has a general disposition to tell the truth. Another is that it tells the truth when it expects you to be able to check. Those explanations make the same predictions on your tests, but very different predictions in the cases where you actually need help.

So I wouldn’t say that some impressive behavior intrinsically demands an explanation. The question is whether there are alternative explanations that fit your observations and would undermine the conclusion you’re trying to draw. And then, can you distinguish those explanations experimentally, or give some other reason to trust one over the other?

r001.rationale: It says that if the goal is only to establish performance in tested conditions, checking that the system works can be enough.

r002.rationale: It selects behaviors for explanation based on whether alternative explanations undermine an intended inference, not on a high degree of surprise.

r003.rationale: It does not mention GPT-4, its parameter count, or correct answers occurring by coincidence.
